Here's how the recommended scenario level is calculated in **Gloomhaven (2nd Edition)**:

---

### Standard / Recommended Difficulty

> At recommended difficulty, the scenario level is equal to the average level of the characters divided by 2 (rounded up).

**Formula:** `(Average character level) ÷ 2`, rounded up.

**Example:** If all characters are level 2, the average level (2) ÷ 2 = 1, so the scenario is level 1. Only once a character reaches level 3 would the scenario level potentially increase.

*(Rulebook, passage 30)*

---

### Solo Mode Adjustment

Because solo play reduces uncertainty and makes coordination easier, the formula is adjusted to increase difficulty:

> Take the average level of all characters in the scenario, then **add 1** before dividing by 2 and rounding up.

**Formula:** `((Average character level) + 1) ÷ 2`, rounded up.

**Example:** With three level 4 characters in normal mode: `(4+4+4) ÷ 3 ÷ 2 = 2`. In solo mode: `(((4+4+4) ÷ 3) + 1) ÷ 2 = 3`.

*(Rulebook, passage 124)*

---

### Important Notes
- The scenario level can always be **set freely from 0–7** at the start of any scenario, regardless of the recommended level.
- Lowering it can help a struggling party; raising it keeps the game challenging.
- Scenario level affects **monster stats**, **trap/hazardous terrain damage**, **gold conversion from money tokens**, and **bonus experience** for completing the scenario.

A *Long Rest* in Gloomhaven (2nd Edition) is performed at **initiative 99**.

A few important clarifications from the official FAQ:

> Your Long Rest takes place at Initiative 99. It is not necessarily last in order; if a game effect pushes a figure's initiative above 99, it will act after your long rest. Your long rest will be performed **before** monster turns on Initiative 99, and is ambiguously timed with other players also acting at 99.

*(This is noted as a change from the Gloomhaven 1st edition FAQ.)*

**Sources:** Rulebook p. 36; GH2 FAQ (updated 2026-04-19)

Here are the steps a character follows when taking a **long rest** in Gloomhaven (2nd Edition), per the Rulebook (p. 36):

---

### How to Declare a Long Rest
During the **Card Selection step**, instead of playing two ability cards, a character may declare a long rest. They play **no cards** for the round — the long rest is their entire turn.

---

### When It Happens
The long rest is performed at **initiative 99**. It acts before monsters on initiative 99, and is ambiguously timed with other players also acting at initiative 99. *(FAQ clarification — this is a change from Gloomhaven 1e.)*

---

### The Three Steps (in order)

1. **Lose one card of your choice** from your discard pile and return all remaining discarded cards to your hand. *(This step is mandatory.)*

2. **Perform "*Heal* 2, self"** *(optional).*

3. **Recover all spent items** *(optional).* Items recovered this way can be used during the same turn they are recovered.

---

### Important Notes
- A long rest can only be declared if the character has **at least two cards in their discard pile**.
- Cards **without lost icons** that are currently in your **active area** count as being in your discard pile for the purpose of eligibility to long rest and are eligible to be the card you lose — but they do **not** have to be returned to your hand when resting.

*(Sources: Rulebook passages 77–78, FAQ)*

Here is the *Wound* condition rule from the **Gloomhaven (2nd Edition) Rulebook** (passage 56, Negative Conditions):

---

> **Wound:** The figure suffers 1 damage at the start of each of their turns. Wound is removed when the figure is healed.

---

### Key points:
- A *Wounded* figure takes **1 damage** at the **start of every one of their turns** for as long as the condition persists.
- *Wound* is removed as soon as the figure receives any *Heal* effect — unlike *Poison*, it does **not** block the healing from restoring hit points.
- It applies to **any figure** — characters and monsters alike.

**Contrast with *Poison*:** *Poison* also goes away when healed, but it prevents the heal from actually restoring HP. *Wound* has no such restriction — the heal both removes *Wound* **and** restores HP normally.

Here is a full breakdown of how *Advantage* works with attack modifier cards in **Gloomhaven (2nd Edition)**:

---

## Advantage & Attack Modifier Cards

*(Rulebook, passage 52)*

### The Basic Rule
> With advantage, the attacker draws two modifiers and uses one of them. A monster always uses the better one, but a **character may use either one**.
> With disadvantage, the attacker draws two modifiers and always uses the worse one.

---

### Rolling Modifiers & Advantage/Disadvantage

The interaction with *rolling modifiers* (cards with a rolling icon) adds some complexity:

- **If the first card drawn is a rolling modifier**, keep drawing one card at a time until you draw a non-rolling card. Then draw **one more** card (ignoring any rolling icon on it).
  - With **advantage**: Keep all initial rolling modifiers **plus** whichever of the final two cards you choose.
  - With **disadvantage**: Discard all initial rolling modifiers and use whichever of the final two cards is **worse**.
- **If the first card is not rolling but the second is**, the rolling icon on the second card is still ignored.

---

### Determining "Better" vs. "Worse" — Ambiguity Rules

*(FAQ, passages 26–27, updated 2026-04-19)*

When comparing two cards, here's how to evaluate them:

- **Non-numeric effects** (conditions like *Stun*, *Shield*, elements, healing, etc.) always have a **positive but unknown value**. They are always considered *at least as good* as a plain numeric bonus of the same amount.
- **Conditional numeric bonuses** (e.g., "+2 if drawn during a Lost action") are evaluated based on the current board state.
- **The x2 modifier** is evaluated using the current attack value (e.g., x2 on an Attack 2 = +2 effective damage, same as a +2 card — making them **ambiguous** in that case).
- **Items like Iron Helm (Item 027)** that modify the drawn card's value are factored in **before** determining better/worse.

**Examples from the FAQ:**
| Draw | Result |
|---|---|
| x2 (Attack 2) vs. +2 | **Ambiguous** (2×2 = 2+2) |
| x2 (Attack 2) vs. +1 | **x2 is better** (2×2 > 2+1) |
| x2 (Attack 2) vs. +2 with Iron Helm | **+2 is better** (Iron Helm turns x2 into +0, so 2+0 < 2+2) |
| +1 Stun vs. +1 | **+1 Stun is better** (Stun has unknown positive value) |
| +0 Stun vs. +2 | **Ambiguous** (unknown value of Stun can't be compared to +2) |

> Note: Even seemingly "negative" effects (like self-damage or a self-condition) are treated as having positive value for ambiguity purposes.

---

### Tie-Breaking Ambiguity

> When there is ambiguity about which modifier is worse, the attacker **must use the one drawn first**.

This matters for *Disadvantage* — if neither card is clearly worse, you are forced to use the first card drawn.

---

**Summary:** *Advantage* = draw 2, pick the better (characters choose freely); *Disadvantage* = draw 2, must use the worse. Rolling modifiers chain further draws. Ambiguous cases (where neither card is clearly better/worse) are resolved by always using the **first card drawn** under *Disadvantage*, and player's choice under *Advantage*.

In **Gloomhaven (2nd Edition)**, a character can bring a number of *Small* items (•) into a scenario **up to half their level, rounded up**.

So the limit scales with character level:

| Character Level | Max Small Items |
|:-:|:-:|
| 1 | 1 |
| 2 | 1 |
| 3 | 2 |
| 4 | 2 |
| 5 | 3 |
| 6 | 3 |
| 7 | 4 |
| 8 | 4 |
| 9 | 5 |

The full item limit per character, as stated in the Rulebook (p. 33), is:

> Each character can bring one **Head** item, one **Body** item, one **Feet** item, one **One Hand** (or one **Two Hands**) item, and a number of **Small** items up to half their level (rounded up).

Here is what the verified tool results say about looting in **Gloomhaven (2nd Edition)**:

---

## Looting

### End-of-Turn Looting

> Characters must loot any money tokens or treasure tiles present in their hex at the end of their turn.

- **Only characters** perform end-of-turn looting. No other figures (monsters, summons, etc.) do.

---

### Money Tokens

- When a money token is looted by a **monster**, nothing else happens.
- When a money token is looted by a **character**, they place the token on their character mat to be converted to gold after the scenario.

---

### Treasure Tiles

- When a treasure tile is looted, it is **removed from the map**.
- **Monsters cannot loot treasure tiles.**
- If the looted treasure tile is a **numbered treasure**, reference that number in the Treasure Index and apply the effect.
- Only the looting character gains the reward — **unless** it is a random item design or random scenario.
- If a looting character gains a copy of an item they **already own**, they must either give it to another character or sell it immediately.

---

### End of Scenario

- If any money tokens or treasure tiles remain on the map when the scenario ends, they **cannot be looted** — looting can only be performed during the scenario.

---

*Sources: Gloomhaven (2nd Edition) Rulebook, passages 64 & 76; FAQ passage 38.*

**Yes, you can skip targets in a red hex AoE attack.** This is directly confirmed by the official FAQ:

> **Can I skip targets in a red hex AoE attack?** Yes; a red hex AoE just determines the hexes where your *potential* targets are. Note — this is a change from the Gloomhaven 1e FAQ, and is to make it consistent with all other non-mandatory targeting.
> — *GH2 FAQ*

So the red hex pattern defines **which hexes are eligible**, but you are not forced to attack every figure that happens to be standing in those hexes. This is consistent with general targeting rules in GH2, where attacking is non-mandatory.

**A couple of related rulings worth knowing:**
- **Line of sight is still required** — only figures within line-of-sight in the red hexes can be targeted.
- **Enemies must be present at the start** of the red hex attack ability — a figure that spawns mid-ability in a red hex cannot be attacked with it.
- **Walls don't block the pattern itself** — the red hex shape applies as-is even across wall lines (though you still need line of sight to each target).
